old: both on the battlefield and on the restless sea
new: both on the field of battle and on the waves of the weary sea
reason: Butler: "both on the field of battle and by the waves of the weary sea"; the same line is accepted at B08-P013 as "on the field of battle and on the waves of the weary sea", and the draft both replaces the epithet (weary → restless) and drops "the waves of" (the drafter's note that Book 8 was unavailable is wrong: book08/candidate-v2.json is in the accepted list).

old: both on the battlefield and on the restless sea
new: both on the field of battle and on the waves of the weary sea
reason: Butler repeats the ¶8 line verbatim: "both on the field of battle and by the waves of the weary sea"; same repair as ¶8 so all three instances (B08-P013, B13-P8, B13-P24) read alike.

old: stone mixing bowls
new: stone mixing-bowls
reason: Butler "mixing bowls"; PUNCTUATION §4 (D15) fixes the hyphenated "mixing-bowl(s)", printed in accepted Books 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 and 11; scripts/compound_drift.py fails on this key ("mixingbowls hyphenated in book01/book02; open in ody").

old: she ran halfway up onto the shore
new: she ran half her own length onto the shore
reason: Butler: "she ran half her own length on to the shore"; "halfway up onto the shore" replaces a stated measure (half the ship's length) with a different, vaguer one.

old: a torn wallet
new: a bag all in holes
reason: Butler: "a staff and a wallet all in holes"; accepted B05-P020 and B09-P011 render Butler's "wallet" as "bag" (to a modern listener a wallet is a billfold, which cannot be slung by a thong), and "torn" drops "all in holes".

old: you’re so persuasive, shrewd, and clever
new: you’re so persuasive, shrewd, and shifty
reason: Butler: "you are so plausible, shrewd and shifty"; "clever" turns Athena's teasing charge of shiftiness into a compliment, softening her characterization (she has just called him a "shifty lying fellow" at ¶25, which the draft keeps).

old: who stays home constantly grieving for you
new: who stays at home grieving for you in vain
reason: Butler: "your wife, who remains at home vainly grieving for you"; "constantly" replaces Butler's qualifier "vainly" (in vain—her grief achieves nothing) with a different one, a change of meaning.

old: by giving me safe passage and these generous gifts
new: by giving me an escort and these generous gifts
reason: Butler: "by giving me an escort"; "escort" is held in every accepted Book (B06-P022, B07-P017/19/25, B08-P002/47, B11-P026/30) and in this Book's ¶4, ¶13, ¶14, ¶17, where the Phaeacians' giving of escorts is the very thing Poseidon punishes.

old: given me safe passage
new: given me an escort
reason: Butler: "given me an escort"; same held word as ¶3.

old: to the blessed gods from where they sat
new: to the blessed gods that live in heaven from where they sat
reason: Butler: "made a drink-offering to the blessed gods that live in heaven"; the epithet is dropped (and "heaven" count falls from 4 to 3 real instances; the draft's fourth match is ¶16's added "Good heavens").

old: the loud-roaring sea
new: the sounding sea
reason: Butler: "the shore of the sounding sea"; accepted B06-P015 keeps "the sounding sea"; "loud-roaring" is an intensified new rendering of the stock epithet.

old: the harbor of old Phorcys the merman
new: the harbor of the old merman Phorcys
reason: Butler: "the haven of the old merman Phorcys", word for word as at ¶9, which the draft renders "the old merman Phorcys"; the drafter's note says both are rendered identically, but they are not.

old: lording it over your house
new: lording it in your house
reason: Butler: "who have been lording it in your house"; the repair is right to restore the idiom but changes the preposition; D29 says a repair restores Butler's own words.

old: how you can deal with these shameless men
new: how you can lay hands on these shameless men
reason: Butler: "think how you can lay hands on these disreputable people"; "deal with" softens the physical threat that ¶33's "blood and brains" makes explicit.

old: cast off the hawser from the mooring stone
new: cast off the hawser from the pierced stone it had been tied to
reason: Butler: "loosed the hawser from the pierced stone to which it had been bound"; the concrete detail "pierced" is dropped (GLOSSARY Voice and form: concrete physical detail kept exactly).

old: claim you
new: lay their hands on you
reason: Butler: "till age and death, the common lot of mankind, lay their hands upon you"; the image of age and death laying hands on her is flattened to "claim".

old: me, who has always been with you
new: me, who have always been with you
reason: Butler: "me, who have been ever with you"; after "me" the verb agrees in the first person ("who have"), and the rest of the clause ("who watched… who made") is hers speaking of herself.

old: Bear everything silently and endure
new: Bear everything and endure
reason: Butler: "Bear everything, and put up with every man's insolence, without a word"; "silently" is added and duplicates Butler's own "without a word" at the end of the sentence.

old: racing across the plain
new: racing over the course
reason: Butler: "as a four in hand chariot flies over the course"; the simile is a chariot race on a racecourse, not across a plain.

old: fresh water always flows within
new: there is always water within
reason: Butler: "at all times there is water within it"; "fresh" and "flows" are details Butler does not state.
